The tracking of those peaks proved to be very sensitive however to the laser excitation wavelength, the local environment and, more importantly, the laser power, which is known to induce local heat in samples thus potentially disturbing the magnetic order. Moreover, it may also be sensitive to alterations in the lattice structure around the Fe as a result of the exfoliation, like strain or damage, which may affect the vibrational spectra but are not straightforwardly connected to the magnetic transition. As an example, a very recent report shows that the Ne el temperature ( T N) in FePS3 can drastically decrease with slight strain 24 and is not necessarily related to the number of layers.

The combination of all these factors resulted in a variety of different Raman spectra in the literature and more importantly showed a disagreement in key aspects of the magnetic properties of exfoliated FePS3. While Wang et al. show a drop in the T N with decreasing thickness of the sample, 14 Lee at al. show no significant variation of T N down to the monolayer limit. 13

This result represents a direct magnetic evidence showing the antiferromagnetic transition in exfoliated FePS3 few-layers flakes (<9 nm). It is interesting to note that the width of the magnetic transition is not significantly broader than in bulk. This may be indicative of a comparable distribution of flake thickness between bulk and LPE flakes. Only a small broadening of the low temperature tail is observed for sample ω 4 , probably pointing to the presence of a significant population of flakes thinner than the average, as hinted by AFM in Figure 2.

The Ne el temperature in the exfoliated samples is obtained as the maximum in the first derivative of the susceptibility with temperature (d χ /d T ), as shown in Figure 3c. In this work, we present a spectroscopic study of few-layer to bulk MnPS3 from cryogenic temperature to room temperature. We propose a formula to quickly and accurately identify the layer numbers of MnPS3 based on optical contrast spectra. All Raman modes are also identi fi ed by polarized Raman measurements. More interesting, we found three magnetic transition temperatures at around 120, 80, and 55 K based on temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy.

The samples were prepared from bulk MnPS3 crystals (about 1 mm) onto Si substrates covered with a SiO2 fi lm of 90 nm using the micromechanical exfoliation technique. Raman measurements and optical contrast measurements were undertaken in backscattering geometry with a JobinYvon HR800 system equipped with a liquid-nitrogen-cooled charge-coupled detector (CCD). The Raman spectra were collected with a 100 × objective lens (NA = 0.9) and a 1800 lines/mm grating at room temperature, while a 50 × longworking-distance objective lens (NA = 0.5) was used for lowtemperature measurements. The excitation wavelength was 488 nm from an Ar + laser. The typical laser power was about 0.17 mW to avoid laser heating on the sample. A tungsten halogen lamp was used as a light source for optical contrast measurements.

hits.text: In summary, we have systematically investigated the magnetic and structural evolution of MnPS3 under high-pressure and low-temperature regimes using high-pressure Raman spectroscopy and DFT calculations. Our findings demonstrate that the Néel temperature is significantly elevated by pressure, rising from 78 K at ambient pressure to 240 K at 20.2 GPa. The concomitant blueshift of a possible two-magnon-related magnetic Raman feature is consistent with the substantial enhancement of magnetic exchange under compression. This enhancement is closely linked to a pressure-induced layer- sliding transition occurring at approximately 5 GPa, which triggers a magnetic reconfiguration from interlayer ferromagnetic to interlayer antiferromagnetic coupling. These insights not only clarify the complex behavior of MnPS3 under extreme conditions but also advance our understanding of two-dimensional magnetic materials, thereby enriching the broader field of condensed matter physics.
